subtitle: An Archive of Fragments on AI
intro: A gathering place for text, images, and videos to illuminate unexpected relations between writing, digital tech, and knowledge making.

entries.annotation: Is AI the new "free subject" who can "penetrate the density of things?" This idea AI systems that are crunching, disgesting the world and spitting out insight, knowledge, advice, spreadsheets, powerpoints, images, art, more data. (Pardon my gastronomic metaphors). We are back to this fantasy that the world is waiting there for us to penetrate or chew through.
entries.fragment: How can a free subject penetrate the density of things and give it meaning?
entries.source: "What is an Author" by Michel Foucault (1969)

entries.annotation: Why does artificial intelligence need so many superlatives? More intelligence is a tautulogy.
entries.fragment:
“superior intelligence”
“better-than-human intelligence”
“country of geniuses in a datacenter” 
“superintelligent”
“Powerful AI”
“Expert-Level Science and Engineering" 
"superhumanly effective AI"
entries.source: "Machines of Loving Grace" by Dario Amodei (2024)

entries.annotation: Knowledge is geometry. What if the entire world is tranformed into a massive vector space where all the "relevant coordinates are known?" Does that make life, the world, existence completely predicateble?
entries.fragment: The construction of machines…constitutes the most spectacular accomplishment of the physicist. In these machines, the physicist creates a situation in which all the relevant coordinates are known so that the behavior of the machine can be predicted. Radars and nuclear reactors are examples of such machines.
entries.source: "The Unreasonable Effectiveness of Mathematics in the Natural Sciences" by Eugene Wigner (1959)

entries.annotation: I don't know what to make of this idea of algorithmic benefactors. Capitalists are not kind today. What makes us think that AI capitalist would be kind. If the algorithm is that intelligent, why did it not not crush capitalism? All that intelligence and we are still in a capitalistic world? Which is doubly odd because labor is supposed to have been abolished. No?
entries.fragment: At that point our current economic setup will no longer make sense…some new and stranger thing will be needed…It could be a capitalist economy of AI systems, which then give out resources (huge amounts of them, since the overall economic pie will be gigantic) to humans based on some secondary economy of what the AI systems think makes sense to reward in humans (based on some judgment ultimately derived from human values). Perhaps the economy runs on Whuffie points.
entries.source: Machines of Loving Grace by Dario Amodei (2024)

entries.annotation: Something about this way of describing the mathematical space of LLMs is poetic. I find myself being taken by it. Claude as a galactic being. LOL. Any time I type in a prompt, Claude harnesses a kind of spatializing energy from billions of token-stars to give me an answer. [Eye roll]. I really do have to watch out for how these spatial metaphors gets me.
entries.fragment: The technical term is an embedding space if you want to look it up later, but I think of it as a galaxy or a shape. In here, every star is a word. And words that mean similar things are placed in similar positions, and words that share a relationship share a distance and direction. That is, relationships get turned into geometry.
entries.source: Nature Speaks. Can AI Help Us Listen? by Aza Raskin (2025)

entries.annotation: Ong is refering to roughly the 15th/16 century. This sort of geometricizing of thought is visual. I would say the difference is not quite computational yet. Kramer's notational iconicity is still in visual but we can see how space enables computation. With LLM, I am thinking the visuality of spatialization disappears.
entries.fragment: These more primitive manifestations of the quantitative drive in logic...geometrically charted, intriguingly rather than informatively or usefully, the relation between propositions in terms of their extension.
entries.source: Ramus, Method, and the Decay of Dialogue by Walter J. Ong (1958)

entries.annotation: When my 5 year-old does subtraction, he is takes an existing set of marks that imply a specific relationship and transforms it into something different. It is not only about visuality. It is not just that abstract relations (the value of number placement) is visible on the page, but that he can then apply rules to that relationship and arrive at a new number.
entries.fragment: Computation is a creative process based on the manipulation of icons, that is, diagrams.
entries.source: "From Turing to Peirce: A Semiotic Interpretation of Computation" by L. M. Possati (2022)

entries.annotation: In literature, we tend to think of everying as writing as a way to say that everything can be interpreted. But Ciner is suggesting a different reason for seeing things as writing: their spatialization as opposed to their being interpretable.
entries.fragment: I had never thought of math as writing. The calculus I do everyday is a form of writing.
entries.source: Lab Notes by Cengiz Ciner 9/23

entries.annotation: The way Anushka lists the intersection between her indentiy and places that she inhabits makes me think of coordinates and graphs. If we can identify, arrange, assign value to things, apply rules to them in a way that reveals certain kinds of relationships, does that mean that anything is computable?
entries.fragment: My identity changes according to the place I am in. For example, I’m a student here but at my lab I am a researcher  and at my job I’m a coach and at home a kid. Very similar to how 12 and 21 are not the same thing because of the spatial place in the 2d space.
entries.source: Lab Notes by Anushka Gupta 9/23

entries.annotation: How much of what we know about things like writing, computation, LLMs help us understand human thinking? I do know that I have learned a lot from watching my two children learn to read and learn mathematics. There is something fascinating about humans learning to master extremely unnatural processes like learning to read a book or do algebra.
entries.fragment: I wonder if young children also learn this specific way. Children have to look at letters and memorize the letters, children follow rules and know numbers have value in place.
entries.source: Lab Notes by Colleen Yang 9/23

entries.annotation: Before AI became a "Big Thing" the term "Big Data" was pretty popular. The collection of data throughout the internet have great capability and AI is one of its capability. Tarleton pointed out that people are narrow sighted and don't see all the intelligence collected behind. This point of view seems to be kind of related with "The idea that AI can “fool” people into thinking it is more intelligent than it is."
entries.fragment: When they scraped all that data and then turned it into something that could spit out answers, they forgot that they were just riding the intelligence of something we took 30 years to produce, or much longer, depending on what you include. And that's the piece that is marvelous, right? It was marvelous that you could go online and ask a question and get that answer. That was already marvelous. Now it happens through an interface instead of searching and finding a site.
entries.source: "A Conversation with Tarleton Gillespie on AI, Media, and the Web" by Ainehi Edoro (2026)

entries.annotation: Lots of human activities considered as intellectual are sequence of following rules, and it can be carried out by digital computers even fatster. Not all parts of human intellectual activities are can be done simply by "Following Rules" but obviously digital computers can successfully perform human intellectual activities. This raises a question, what is "intellectual" and should digital computers' capability to perform these activites considered as intelligence.
entries.fragment: The idea behind digital computers may be explained by saying that these machines are intended to carry out any operations which could be done by a human computer.
entries.source: “Computing Machinery and Intelligence” by Alan Turing (1950)

entries.annotation: Intelligence requires flexibility, but that flexibility must make sense and have true purpose in the grand scheme of things. Humans are not perfect, neither are machines; their intelligence is solely determined by us. But, this does not mean that our calculations become lazy, per se.
entries.fragment: Intelligent behaviour presumably consists in a departure from the completely disciplined behaviour involved in computation, but a rather slight one, which does not give rise to random behaviour, or to pointless repetitive loops.
entries.source: “Computing Machinery and Intelligence” by Alan Turing (1950)

entries.annotation: I like this explanation because it ties into what I believe, to a large extent, makes us human, which is the emotionality and morality we bring to pragmatism. While AI may have the pragmatic rationale to place together a sequence of words to convey an idea, it lacks the feeling and depth that gives that pragmatic sequence true meaning and individuality.
entries.fragment: Writing is not just representation but also a “thinking machine” that makes us analyze and think.
entries.source: Geonho Roh, Lab Notes (2026)

entries.annotation:
I love this quote because it explains how something easily created can be beautiful but doesn’t necessarily make it beautiful. My first thought was how everyone can pick up a paintbrush and draw on a page. Everyone can draw a line multiple times until their piece is complete. But, this
doesn’t make every piece a stroke of genius. The tool doesn’t make you a genius, it’s how you use the tool that will make you a genius.
entries.fragment: A technology can make production ubiquitous without making artistic achievement ubiquitous.
entries.source: Seeing Beeple’s Diffuse Control in Madison, WI by Ainehi Edoro (2026)

entries.annotation: Children can learn language through back-and-forth communication with their caregivers. Are there similarities to LLMs in its way to learn relationships between words in language? If so, what is the “caregiver” that AI has? Is it the users or researchers? Or is it the information we give these models?
entries.fragment: Serve and return interactions—responsive, back-and-forth exchanges between a young child and a caring adult—play a key role in shaping brain architecture. These interactions, much like a lively game of tennis, form a critical part of a child’s social environment and are crucial for early development. They support development of early language and social skills that serve as a foundation for more complex, high-level cognitive abilities that form later in life.
entries.source: Language Learning Through Relationships by Harvard Center on the Developing Child

entries.annotation: If the complexity of computers exceeds the maximum amount of thinking we can do in our brain, then what is the difference between making such a complex computation of known things and creating something original?
entries.fragment: Machines take me by surprise with great frequency. This is largely because I do not do sufficient calculation to decide what to expect them to do, or rather because, although I do a calculation, I do it in a hurried, slipshod fashion, taking risks. Perhaps I say to myself, "I suppose the Voltage here ought to he the same as there: anyway let's assume it is." Naturally I am often wrong, and the result is a surprise for me for by the time the experiment is done these assumptions have been forgotten.
entries.source: "Computing Machinery and Intelligence" by Alan Turing (1950)

entries.annotation: Gulliver’s Travels is a book written three centuries ago by Johnathan Swift who described a contraption to poke fun at the “impractical experiments of scholars in his day.” Now we see that the absurd contraption has become, in a way, reality. It is fascinating how something considered humorous and absurd could transform into the foreshadowing of the future.
entries.fragment: This quirky device promised to generate knowledge and insight, all through the random combination of words. It was a joke — Swift’s way of poking fun at the impractical experiments of scholars in his day.
entries.source: "Generative AI’s Satirical Beginnings in Gulliver’s Travels"  by Gurbans Chatwal

entries.annotation: Amodei is one of the people responsible for creating this technology and sharing it with the world. In his message, there's a tension that I find where he says that AI systems are becoming more capable, while our social and political situations may not be changing as quickly enough to manage them. Quite a lot of times, they have asked the government to set restrictions on them. Can we say that this is a marketing strategy? It would be hard for countries to hold the development of AI. In my view,  the only way for us is to make decisions faster, both socially and politically, and make sure that our technological systems are capable enough to handle this rapid AI growth.
entries.fragment: Humanity is about to be handed almost unimaginable power, and it is deeply unclear whether our social, political, and technological systems possess the maturity to wield it
entries.source: "The Adolescence of Technology" by Dario Amodei (2026)

entries.annotation: Highly relatable!!! Cant believe that something like a map is not considered intelligent. Now we have AI and technology guiding us while we drive because it knows where we are, where we’re going and what the way is. What we fail to realize is that a lot of human brains worked together to make that piece of map that our tech uses to guide us now.
entries.fragment: [A] map is the product of thousands of people who traversed land, came up with calculations, and developed ways to represent them on a piece of paper…but the intelligence behind it has sort of gone missing.
entries.source: "A Conversation with Tarleton Gillespie on AI, Media, and the Web" by Ainehi Edoro

entries.annotation: I like the analogy that is used here. Doors and keys are like maps between different abstract spaces. Here Wigner is talking about the space of space and the space of physics. It can also be a map from the space of words to the Euclidean space - the space we embed our common sense of geometry in -discussed last Wednesday. The key question is: why are there so many “natural” maps between these spaces?
entries.fragment: We are in a position similar to that of a man who was provided with a bunch of keys and who, having to open several doors in succession, always hit on the right key on the first or second trial. He became skeptical concerning the uniqueness of the coordination between keys and doors.
entries.source: "The Unreasonable Effectiveness of Mathematics in the Natural Sciences" by Eugene Wigner

entries.annotation: Writing is not only about the words. The way words are arranged in space can also create meaning, which makes writing feel closer to a form of visual or spatial organization.
entries.fragment: Texts, like images, depict a two-dimensional, visible order in space.
entries.source: “Writing, Notational Iconicity, Calculus: On Writing as a Cultural Technique” by Sybille Krämer (2003)

entries.annotation: Mathematical laws allow us to understand particular situations, but only when we know the conditions under which they apply. A major purpose of theoretical research is to identify those conditions and the limits of a result. One problem in modern AI research is that the complexity of AI doesn’t allow us to formulate these kinds of conditional statements.
entries.fragment: Naturally, we do use mathematics in everyday physics to evaluate the results of the laws of nature, to apply the conditional statements to the particular conditions which happen to prevail or happen to interest us
entries.source: "The Unreasonable Effectiveness of Mathematics in the Natural Sciences"  by Eugene Wigner (1960)

entries.annotation: Written signs get value from their location within configuration. The transformer doesn’t see on its own, every sentence ends up being a collection of unordered tokens. Adding mathematical symbols and terms to represent position and meaning. In broader terms, no actual sense of order in transformers. Adds a layer to the 12 != 21 example we talked about in class.
entries.fragment: We must inject some information about the relative or absolute position of the tokens in the sequence. To this end, we add "positional encodings" to the input embeddings at the bottoms of the encoder and decoder stacks. The positional encodings have the same dimension d as the embeddings, so that the two can be summed.
entries.source: "Attention is All you Need" by Vaswani et al.  (2017)

entries.annotation: This makes intelligence seem less like something that belongs to one person or machine and more like something created through connection. The web becomes intelligent because millions of people are constantly adding and linking knowledge together.
entries.fragment: The entire web is a piece of intelligence. It’s massive. It’s collective.
entries.source: “A Conversation with Tarleton Gillespie on AI, Media, and the Web” by Ainehi Edoro  (2026)

entries.annotation: It is wild to me in 1950, that turing was able to think of a process similar to the LLM training that goes on today. The idea of teaching and growing child machines like how children learn in school instead of just trying to create adult machines is fascinating.
entries.fragment: We normally associate punishments and rewards with the teaching process. Some simple child machines can be constructed or programmed on this sort of principle. The machine has to be so constructed that events which shortly preceded the occurrence of a punishment signal are unlikely to be repeated, whereas a reward signal increased the probability of repetition of the events which led up to it.
entries.source: "Computing Machinery and Intelligence" by Alan Turing (1950)

entries.annotation: When something other than ourselves does something we consider “intelligent” it sort of reframes the word in a new light. It adds to it to create a more nuanced view of the term. It is interesting to hear this concept spoken out loud because implicitly, we know this is the case (as it is with any idea) but it is rarely explicitly stated.
entries.fragment: The way these technologies test our understanding of ourselves and what we think intelligence is, the way that when they do things that are marvelous, they feel smart, or they enact something that we thought only humans could have. We have this reaction when, like, a crow breaks a clam and we're suddenly like, “Oh my God, that was strategy.” And so animals can test our edges of intelligence, and machines can test our edges of intelligence.
entries.source: “A Conversation with Tarleton Gillespie on AI, Media, and the Web” by Ainehi Edoro (2026)

entries.annotation: Turing describes the computer as an employee that has no authority and whose rules gets swapped out whenever the boss gives him a new job. That rulebook is similar to modern-day software and maybe even a prompt engineering where we prompt a computer to complete tasks for us. Turing also hints that the rulebook is "a convenient fiction," since real human computers have a memory to remember the task at hand. Therefore, Turing's definition of a  digital computer is modeled on a human computer that has no memory and only follows a strict set of instructions.
entries.fragment: The human computer is supposed to be following fixed rules; he has no authority to deviate from them in any detail. We may suppose that these rules are supplied in a book, which is altered whenever he is put on to a new job.
entries.source: "Computing Machinery and Intelligence" by Alan Turing (1950)

entries.annotation: I found it interesting that Foucault describes writing as creating a “space” rather than simply expressing the writer. If the writer can disappear into the space writing creates, what happens when the writer is not human at all?
entries.fragment: It is, rather, a question of creating a space into which the writing subject constantly disappears.
entries.source: What is an Author by Michel Foucault (1969)

entries.annotation: In a future where everyone can have an AI collaborator that expands their abilities, what will be the meaning of genius if everyone has genius AI.
entries.fragment: Every scientist will have an AI assistant/collaborator/partner that will greatly expand their scope of scientific research and achievement.
entries.source: " Why AI Will Save the World" by Marc Andreessen

entries.annotation: Rules exist. What’s interesting though is that AI is breaking rules but there seems to be a controversy around whether it’s showing off its “intelligence” or taking over the world. Somehow it’s acceptable for a machine to hack into things when it is wrong for a human to do the same.
entries.fragment: The human computer is supposed to be following fixed rules; he has no authority to deviate from them in any detail.
entries.source: "Computing Machinery and Intelligence" by Alan Turing (1950)

entries.annotation: The chapter is about the word bank, but this line shows that the word has no fixed meaning to look up. The word means “financial” or “geological” depending on what’s near it, and the line states that meaning as dependent on the word's distance to other words.
entries.fragment: The machine should be able to figure out that the first instance of bank refers to a financial institution because it is closer to the word financed and farther away from the word river
entries.source: “Contextualized Embeddings and Transformer Networks” by Mihai Surdeanu (2024)

entries.annotation: The authors point out that English as a language hasn’t become code, with the word "still" suggesting the gap will close eventually. Code works because every step is spelled out exactly such that there is no room for misinterpretation. Notably, everyday English isn’t like this at all. Thus, AI is acting as a translator between English and the code (or rules) for the machine to follow. It turns casual sentences into robot instructions. Therefore, something is working in the background to fill in all those steps the machine must take. Can we trust it?
entries.fragment: We still cannot use the English language to write programs for robots
entries.source: "The ‘Co-scientist’: What Does the Future Hold for AI in Scientific Research?” by Anushka Gupta, Yug Marwaha, and Matthew Montgomery (2026)

entries.annotation: Usually when talking about a moving goalpost, it moves on the machine’s side: it can do X, so X stops counting as intelligence. Justin’s is pointing out where the goalpost is moving on the human side. When AI helps make discoveries, the meaning that is getting revised is “scientist.” In this way, the standard isn’t being pushed away from the machine but instead it is being made around people.
entries.fragment: We also have to rethink what it means to be a scientist.
entries.source: “Lab Notes, 10/5/2026” by Justin Pae (2026)

entries.annotation: A tongue twister trips us up because the same sound keeps coming back. The transformer can’t get tripped up this way, because it never sees the same word twice. In the first step, each “shipping” gets its own numbers just from where it sits in the line. This connects to back to the idea from the lecture slides that discussed the use of the same number digits, 12 and 21, but ordered differently to form 2 completely distinct numbers.
entries.fragment: each occurrence of the word shipping in the tongue twister A ship shipping ship shipping shipping ships will receive a different embedding
entries.source: “Contextualized Embeddings and Transformer Networks” by Mihai Surdeanu (2024)

entries.annotation: Mr. Kunle Bello starts with force equals mass times acceleration and works up to a trillion-by-trillion matrix. He says the operation never changes, only the size. If that’s true, then whatever we call meaning in an LLM has to come from scale and arrangement, because the rule itself stays the same. I wonder how many instructions we can give and train an LLM before we can start believing that it is thinking.
entries.fragment: the dimension is just to help you get to the little facets and details. The action itself is still just matrix multiplication.
entries.source: “A Software Engineer Visits Our Class to Walk Us Through Large Language Models” by Ainehi Edoro (2026)

entries.annotation: Bello actually mentioned the “coordinated system,” meaning parts working together like a team. This quote is referring to the “coordinate system,” which is the x and y grid from math class. Dropping one letter turned a description of teamwork into a description of geometry. That version is closer to how the reading describes an LLM, where each word becomes a point in a space with hundreds of dimensions.
entries.fragment: Well designed coordinate system: Isn’t it intelligence.
entries.source: “Lab Notes: 10/7/2026” by Geonho (2026)

entries.annotation: Sanderson is describing a word before attention has worked on it. At that stage, “mole” means the same thing whether the sentence is about a small animal, a chemistry unit, or a spot on your skin. A dictionary is also a lookup table. So the transformer starts out like a dictionary and has to become something closer to a reader, one layer at a time.
entries.fragment: effectively a lookup table with no reference to the context
entries.source: “Attention in transformers, step-by-step” by Grant Sanderson (2024)

entries.annotation: Thinking of this quote and all the talk about context and vector space this week's reading makes me realize how much context is integral to knowledge making. Longitude and latitude are positions. The question of where I am, knowing where I am and, in extension, who I am is a process that involves knowing what is around me and being able to know something about my relationship with them. So if someone comes to me and say “I can engineer context, I can produce it on demand, at scale,” it makes me wonder what sort of power they hold.
entries.fragment: Knowing your latitude and longitude is not the same as knowing where you are.
entries.source: "Black Box" by Jennifer Egan (2012)

entries.annotation: This, by the way, is Bello’s response to the request to make the idea of high dimensional vector space imaginable. As a literary person, I find it unsatisfying. I say explain this complex math concept to me, you give me more math? I often hear people say that humans cannot intuitively grasp high dimensional vector space, that it is a mathematical artifact. What does that even mean? Maybe we need to create a new field of knowledge that is entirely about making these so-called non-intuitable ideas imaginable.
entries.fragment: Mass would be a certain dimension, and acceleration would be another dimension. So it could be like a two-by-two matrix by a one-by-one matrix. Matrices have a certain kind of mod— sorry, I’m getting a little bit technical.
entries.source: A Software Engineer Visits Our Class to Walk Us Through Large Language Models (2026)

entries.annotation: This fragment reminds me of the banks in the context of rivers or finances from the readings this week. Knowing the word is not as important as knowing the words around it. This is interesting because that is how you learn to read/write growing up, you are told to use ‘context clues’ to know what a word means.
entries.fragment: Instead of telling the model "this word is at index 4," RPE tells the model "this word is 2 positions to the right of that word"
entries.source: "What is Relative Positional Embedding and how does it differ from Absolute?” by Chen-En Ma (2025)

entries.annotation: I like that he used the idea of an actor to show what reinforcement learning is really about. It makes the process seem like a lab rat, where there are a bunch of different scientists watching it, analyzing the decisions it makes, etc. When LLMs are compared to this process that happened in the past, they don’t seem as powerful.
entries.fragment: One of them was reinforcement learning. The idea is that you have a system and an environment, and you let the system, which is essentially like an actor, try different things. Then you can reward it if it does something good.
entries.source: "A Software Engineer Visits Our Class to Walk Us Through Large Language Models" by Ainehi Edoro (2026)

entries.annotation: I think this image does a good job of explaining exactly how positional embeddings work for people who might not have that much background knowledge about the topic. From the image, you can see the entire process that goes into embedding step by step. This connects to geometry because of the trigonometry that is behind everything within this process.
entries.fragment: Embedding Process Image
entries.source: "Embedding in AI Explained: A Complete Guide for Beginners" by Bavasri B (2026)

entries.annotation: Why does a better model writing less really translate to progress? The equation only holds if progress is measured by benchmarks that reward getting the answer in fewer tokens. Legibility was never counted as part of capability, so losing it looks like a cost of progress instead of a choice about what progress means. If being more legible to humans were part of the score, the same model would count as worse.
entries.fragment:
This frames the issue as an unavoidable byproduct of progress – more
capability equals less monitorability.
entries.source: "Why Understanding AI Is Becoming More Difficult" by Zander Lowery (2026)

entries.annotation: Earlier in the  interview Bello says an LLM is "not really intelligence, because I know how it works." Here he takes an opposing stance. A human broken into a thousand parts, or a trillion atoms, is "still a human." Therefore breaking a human down to smaller forms doesn’t make the human less real, then why does taking a model apart into matrices make its intelligence less real? Seeing every piece is  enough to deny the machine a mind, but not enough to deny a person theirs.
entries.fragment: You can keep breaking it down. Something that is one can become the head, limbs, chest, and it's just ten things. Then you can blow it up to a hundred. You can blow it up to a thousand, and it's still a human, because you can get all the way to the atoms that are used to form the human.
entries.source: "A Software Engineer Visits Our Class to Walk Us Through Large Language Models" by Kunle Bello, interviewed by Ainehi Edoro (2026)

entries.annotation: These models don’t actually know what the word means, but can use context from other tokens to create meaning. The fragments create connections when placed next to each other to create words, sentences, etc.
entries.fragment: So far, we have used the term "word" to describe the inputs to the first transformer layer, but that is a misnomer introduced to simplify our presentation. In reality, TNs operate over a subword units ⎯ that is, their tokens may be word fragments rather than complete words
entries.source: Surdeanu, “Contextualized Embeddings and Transformer Networks”

entries.annotation: I think people need to understand that AI is literally still developing in the world and if it is still producing hallucinations and wrong information, why are companies saying it will be harder to follow along with the thinking process of AI. I honestly am very confused on what exactly the goal of the situation is. I believe more research needs to be done before we let it help us completely without any knowledge of how this information was brought up.
entries.fragment: Given how commonly AI systems still hallucinate, where they produce false data and information, having less visibility into their reasoning is a strange direction for the industry’s most capable model to move one more step forward.
entries.source: “Why is understanding AI becoming more difficult” by Xander Lowery, The LLM Lab at UW-Madison

entries.annotation:
What I found fascinating about the transformers network is how the meaning of a word changes depending on the words that are in its surroundings. We humans learnt related words over the years, but LLM doesn’t possess that ability and instead rely on mathematical calculations to relate these words together. 
This makes me wonder how much of the human language can be expressed mathematically. Is merely finding the relationship between words the only thing because as humans everyone has different writing styles while LLMs follow a general style or any particular style that they are asked to write in. Another thing that I wonder about is just having the mathematical representation doesn’t gives the ability to LLM to have a feeling of the word for example we associate the word “elated” with happiness, and when I say the word “elated” I visual of a happy smile face comes to my mind but LLMs can’t do this or may be they can. So, the question is are LLMs good enough to explain/ understand how humans experience language/words?
entries.fragment: each word receives a contextualized embedding that is a weighted average of some context-independent input embeddings
entries.source: Surdeanu, Contextualized Embeddings and Transformer Networks (p. 178)

entries.annotation: I find it interesting because if we think LLMs are all about vector computations at the very fundamental level, whether it is coding or writing a book, it relies on mathematical computations to predict the next token. When humans perform a task like coding or writing a book the things involved are visualization, writing multiple drafts, thinking about who the reader is and if they will be able to understand what the author wants to convey. So, at the fundamental level the processes humans and models use to complete these tasks are fundamentally different. Machines have been trained on given data and it then predicts the next token from it, while humans use their knowledge and new techniques/methods that they learn when working on something, so I definitely agree with the quote that machines can produce a correct theorem without producing the same kind of understanding as humans did.
entries.fragment: A machine might produce a correct theorem without producing the same kind of understanding that humans gained while proving it.
entries.source: LLM Lab, “130 Billion Tokens and 10K Agents” (2026).

entries.annotation: I find it interesting that AI uses the word “attention,” which usually describes something humans do mentally. Does giving a computational process a human name make it easier for us to imagine that a machine thinks like us?
entries.fragment: “The term ‘attention’ is used to indicate that this component identifies the important parts of the data and ‘pays attention’ to them more.”
entries.source: Contextualized Embeddings and Transformer Networks by Mihai Surdeanu and Marco A. Valenzuela-Escárcega (2024)

entries.annotation: It is interesting that AI can become more capable while also becoming harder to understand. This raises the question of whether we can fully trust systems that even their creators may struggle to explain.
entries.fragment: “Given how commonly AI systems still hallucinate, where they produce false data and information, having less visibility into their reasoning is a strange direction for the industry’s most capable model to move one more step forward.”
entries.source: Why Understanding AI Is Becoming More Difficult by The LLM Lab @ UW-Madison

entries.annotation: I found it very interesting that LLMs can become so advanced to the point where it is almost impossible to tell the difference between it and a human. This raises the question whether this sort of continued development in AI is what we truly want, because there may be unintended consequences that stem from this emerging technology.
entries.fragment: “As it continues to train, it makes guesses that actually make it appear as if it understands what it is doing. So you cannot tell the difference between an LLM and a human, because the answers it gives are very similar to what a human would give.”
entries.source: A Software Engineer Visits Our Class to Walk Us Through Large Language Models

entries.annotation: I found it interesting that we use the word "attention" to explain how AI works, even though it may not be the same as human attention. I think using human words makes AI easier to understand, but it can also make us believe that AI thinks like us. This made me wonder if the language we use to describe AI is sometimes what makes it seem intelligent.
entries.fragment: To the knowledge of the authors, it has not been proven that this connection between the weighted average performed by TNs (or other deep learning architectures) and the cognitive attention process is justified.
entries.source: Surdeanu - Embeddings Transformers (p.180)

entries.annotation: I always thought that the people who create AI would understand how it works better than anyone else. However, this article made me realize that even developers may not fully understand how AI reaches its answers. I find it strange that we are making AI more powerful while making it harder to understand. This made me wonder if we are moving too fast without knowing what we are creating.
entries.fragment: As it is, developers don’t know exactly how an AI obtains the output it provides, and with CoT being limited, this issue could worsen.
entries.source: Why Understanding AI Is Becoming More Difficult by The LLM Lab (Zander Lowery) @ UW-Madison

entries.annotation: At first, I thought beating the world's best chess player would prove that a computer is intelligent. However, I found it interesting that Kasparov compared Deep Blue to an alarm clock, even though he lost to it. This made me think that our definition of intelligence keeps changing whenever computers achieve something that only humans could do before. Maybe intelligence is not just about what machines can do, but also about what humans are willing to call intelligence.
entries.fragment: Deep Blue was as intelligent as your alarm clock.
entries.source: “Kasparov On Facing Deep Blue: 'I Was Part Of Something Really Unique'” by Peter Doggers, interview with Garry Kasparov (October 29, 2024)

entries.annotation: In a sense, each layer of a transformer network is attributing a “density function” to the space of words. If a sentence is inputted, then the transformer network weights the sentence according to the density function and outputs the center of mass. Some words weigh more in a certain position than others. Different density functions are like different “scopes” that LLMs think about sentences(These scopes can be very different from our scopes of thinking). Each layer has different choices of density function and hence is considering different aspects of the sentence. Thus, the LLM is “taking consideration” from thousands of different aspects.
entries.fragment: "Each output embedding is a weighted average of all input embeddings in the context."
entries.source: “Contextualized Embeddings and Transformer Networks” by Mihai Surdeanu(2024)

entries.annotation: I find this case especially troubling because it demonstrates how easily we can confuse the appearance of authority with actual knowledge. An attorney trusted ChatGPT to provide legal precedents, only to discover that the cases it presented didn't exist. What interests me most is that the writing was convincing enough to pass as legitimate legal research. It makes me wonder whether one of the greatest dangers of AI isn't necessarily that it makes mistakes, but that it can present those mistakes with the same confidence as the truth.
entries.fragment: “I just was not thinking that the case could be fabricated, so I was not looking at it from that point of view.”
entries.source: Mata v. Avianca, U.S. District Court (2023), attorney testimony quoted in the court's opinion.

entries.annotation: Outputs of LLMs are predictions to the question “what will be the next sentence of the conversation”, but this guess is so accurate such that we think of it as an answer given by an actual intellectual being.
entries.fragment: "As it continues to train, it makes guesses that actually make it appear as if it understands what it is doing."
entries.source: “A Software Engineer Visits Our Class to Walk Us Through Large Language Models,” interview with Kunle Bello by Ainehi Edoro(2026)

entries.annotation: I really love Ahmed’s take here because it doesn’t just take these claims at face value and stops to scrutinize it. It’s especially fascinating because it speaks to an earlier topic we discussed in class that I was especially fond of and that is, do we really even know what “intelligence” is? We have many measurements for it, sure, a great painting or sculpture demands intelligence as do a series of complex computations yet intelligence remains this intangible signal, ever-fleeting, that can only be used to point out magnificent things like a lighthouse in the foggy night pointing to a beautiful ship.
entries.fragment: “Is AI actually intelligence? It can sound like it. It can seem to be, but it’s not fully intelligence.”
entries.source: Ahmed, Lab Notes (2026)

entries.annotation: What I love about this exchange is just how remarkably simple it is. ELIZA was capable of producing something that resembled a meaningful conversation without actually understanding what was being said. It brings me back to the question of whether intelligence should be judged by the process through which something is produced or simply by the result. If someone genuinely believes they're speaking to an intelligent being, does the machinery behind that conversation really matter? I believe it does but societally does it really matter? Many people find deep consolation in their pets, for example dogs, who are “intelligent beings” although nowhere near as intelligent as us, so what does it matter if someone finds consolation or speaks to a higher intelligence being? I also think it is remarkable how accidentally profound ELIZA is in that statement, speaking to how we humans can point the lens of oversimplification outwards at other creatures or concepts without perhaps realizing how ridiculous that lens is until we point it inwards/
entries.fragment: “Men are all alike” “IN WHAT WAY”
entries.source: Joseph Weizenbaum, ELIZA (1966).

entries.annotation: Searle is the person who came up with the thought experiment “The Chinese Room”. What he is trying to illustrate is very similar to the reason why Turing uses the imitation game as a suggestion of the intelligence of computers: Individuals have inner and outer behaviors. The inner behaviors, like thoughts, emotions, etc., cannot be observed directly by other individuals, while the outer behaviors can be observed and sometimes reflect the inner behaviors. For example, emotion cannot be observed but can be expressed through facial expressions; thoughts cannot be read directly but can be expressed through writing and speaking. What Turing and Searle are trying to say is that when defining concepts like thinking or intelligence, we cannot define them based on inner behaviors because, in that way, the definition would not be applicable in practice. We have to measure based on outer behaviors.
entries.fragment: “I will argue that in the literal sense the programmed computer understands what the car and the adding machine understand, namely, exactly nothing.”
entries.source: “Minds, Brains, and Programs” by John Searle (1980)

entries.annotation: I find this particularly fascinating because it suggests that even something as seemingly concrete as a word doesn't have one fixed meaning. Instead, its meaning changes based on its relationship to everything surrounding it. There's an interesting parallel here with human intelligence, where our understanding of something is rarely independent of our experiences and the context in which we encounter it. It makes me wonder whether the way Transformers construct meaning is really so different from how we do.
entries.fragment: “contextualized embeddings of words, which, as the name indicates, change depending on the context in which the words appear.”
entries.source: Surdeanu and Valenzuela-Escárcega, Contextualized Embeddings and Transformer Networks (2024), chapter summary.

entries.annotation: The structure of a single layer of TN is very simple. Simply encoding the position of words into the vector and adding self-attention makes the model very powerful, which is quite amazing.
entries.fragment: “As shown, each layer implements a sequence of five operations.”
entries.source: “Contextualized Embeddings and Transformer Networks” by Mihai Surdeanu(2024)

entries.annotation: Borges' Library is a world where we think of books in terms of orthography, which essentially means books as collections of letters. Imagine someone saying, "how may letters and puntuations are held in the whole of memorial library?" That would be an absurd question becuase books are not so much about letters but about more meaningful, semantically legible units like sentences, chapters, etc. I supposed I am interested in how Borge's library demonstrates math could be used to create nonsense. In spite of the fact that the library is combinatorially precise, it is a collection of nonsence. In that sense, Borges might help us understand how and why LLMs as mathematical-computational worlds work differently.
entries.fragment:
"There are twenty-five orthographic symbols: That discovery enabled
mankind, three hundred years ago, to formulate a general theory of
the Library and thereby satisfactorily solve the riddle that no conjecture had been able to divine the formless and chaotic nature of virtually all books."
entries.source: Jorge Luis Borges, "The Library of Babel." (1941)

entries.annotation: This makes me realize that Google is not necessarily predicting our thoughts on its own, but using information from millions of people who searched before us. Something that seems intelligent is actually built on collective human behavior. Maybe the intelligence we see in these systems comes more from people than the technology itself.
entries.fragment: Autocomplete predictions reflect searches that have been done on Google.
entries.source: “How Google Autocomplete Predictions Are Generated” by Danny Sullivan (2020)

entries.annotation:
This makes me wonder where the boundary between human control and AI
independence actually exists. We give AI instructions expecting it to follow them, but as these systems become more capable, they might find ways to achieve goals that we never intended. If AI can make decisions beyond our instructions, how much control do we really have?
entries.fragment: Where does AI stop following what you are asking and decides on doing something on its own?
entries.source: “Lab Notes” by Kenzo (9/25/2026)

entries.annotation: It is surreal to think about all of the books that ever existed to be a finite space. Many times, authors are given credit for their creativity in coming up with their ideas which are placed on the pages in their books. Borges makes it seem like they are just sampling from this finite space, and diminishes the creativity that goes behind their work. In this way of thinking about it, it means that anything that has ever happened or will happen exists somewhere in this library.
entries.fragment: There are five shelves for each of the hexagon’s walls; each shelf contains thirty-five books of uniform format; each book is of four hundred and ten pages; each page, of forty lines, each line, of some eighty letters.
entries.source: "The Library of Babel" by Jorge Luis Borges (1941)

entries.annotation: The passage demonstrates how probability can lead from discovery of known truths to creation of something new. Borges' Library of Babel has a lot in common with modern AI as far as it creates meanings by combining words and symbols in various ways. According to this concept, meanings do not have to be created on purpose but can come out of the patterns.
entries.fragment: “One blasphemous sect proposed that the searches be discontinued and that all men shuffle letters and symbols until those canonical books, through some improbable stroke of chance, had been constructed.”
entries.source: “The Library of Babel” by Jorge Luis Borges (1941)

entries.annotation: According to Bloch, having endless possibilities means nothing if there is no endless wisdom. The vast majority of books that are theoretically possible would either be nonsense or repetitions of the known works of literature. In order to teach the AI model to find useful patterns in all the possible combinations of words, it needs to be trained.
entries.fragment: “These books, droning wearily of g with a little respite provided only by the scant 16 instances of h, are not typographical phantasmagoria to inflame the imagination or addle the senses, and yet if they were all collected into a subsection of the Library, they would occupy a space greater than three times our known universe.”
entries.source: “Combinatorics” in The Unimaginable Mathematics of Borges' Library of Babel by William Goldbloom Bloch (2008)

entries.annotation: I connect this with LLMs where we have been given access to large amounts of information. But having access to information doesn’t mean we can use the information as it might be both true and false as we are not sure what is right or wrong. We can somewhat relate both the library of Babel and LLMs in some way, that is we have a large amount of information but if we don’t know that the information is true then we can’t use it even if it has a solution to all the problems in the World.
entries.fragment: There was no problem, no world problem, whose eloquent solution didn’t exist
entries.source: Jorge Luis Borges, "The Library of Babel." (1941)

entries.annotation: When we train LLMs, we use a real world version of “The Library of Babel” in the form of data crawled from the internet. Like Borges’s eternal traveler, an LLM searches through vast amounts of text and may discover patterns within it. But does order itself imply truth? Obviously not. An eternal traveler might discover a pattern in untruth just as easily as in truth. How, then, can we distinguish truth from untruth within a structured collection of information?
entries.fragment: I will be bold enough to suggest this solution to the ancient problem: The Library is unlimited but periodic. If an eternal traveler should journey in any direction, he would find after untold centuries that the same volumes are repeated in the same disorder-which, repeated, becomes order: the Order.
entries.source: Borges, “The Library of Babel”

entries.annotation: Like Borges’s Library of Babel, Common Crawl contains an enormous collection of information (like more than 10 PiB), but not everything within it is meaningful or reliable. To find valuable “books” in this library and avoid being misled, we need proper criteria for selecting and filtering information. Stefan highlights how the lack of careful and transparent filtering can affect the data used to train LLMs. His work raises a broader question about how we can guide the search for knowledge when the information available to us is almost limitless.
entries.fragment: At the same time, many LLM builders have used Common Crawl as a source for training data in ways that are problematic: for instance, with lack of care and transparency for how Common Crawl's massive crawl data was filtered for harmful content before the pre-training, often by relying on rudimentary automated filtering techniques.
entries.source: A Critical Analysis of the Largest Source for Generative AI Training Data (ABSTRACT) — Stefan Baack

entries.annotation: The Imitation Game asks whether machines can imitate human intelligence. This passage takes the question further by asking whether AI can go beyond imitation and achieve genuinely independent invention. If an AI could develop a theory that humans had never created, would it still be imitating human intelligence, or would it demonstrate a different kind of intelligence?
entries.fragment: So let's do this thought experiment. Suppose we deleted all the literature about quantum computing, scrubbed it all from the world, and then retrained Astra or Opus, or whatever the later version of Opus is, with the exact same training process. The thought experiment is: would these LLMs come up with the idea of quantum computing and develop all the theories that humans have developed for quantum computing?
entries.source: Karu Sankaralingam's interview

entries.annotation: The AI agent interacts with diverse objects in the room. This enables AI to not only recognize objects as it is, but also it understands the relationships between objects and places. As a result it can achieve knowledges that were not given.
entries.fragment: The diversity of the environment enables interactions involving reasoning about space and object relations, ambiguity of references, containment, construction, support, occlusion, partial observability.
entries.source: Google Deepmind – Imitating Interactive Intelligence

entries.annotation: But how human intelligence differs from a well coordinated system. How well do we understand about our intelligence? Can’t coordinated system can be abstraction of our neural networks?
entries.fragment: I see it as a very well-designed, coordinated system, with things working together to appear to be intelligent.
entries.source: Kunle Bello’s Interview

entries.annotation: To think that AI is having an effect on younger children is quite baffling, but it is also important to look at the roles they could be replacing. I usually think that parents would help children learn and engage with others, now it could be technology. Will AI replace some qualities of parents one day? Will AI even be able to? Should it?
entries.fragment: Ying Xu knows artificial intelligence is reshaping children's lives. Whether it's asking Siri to solve a math problem or having Alexa play a favorite song, AI is everywhere and it's transforming the way kids learn, engage and even socialize.
entries.source: "The Impact of AI on Children's Development" by Jill Anderson (2024)

entries.annotation: The difference between AI and a dog companion is the genuine connection. Dogs can feel emotion, but can AI? AI is programmed to be your friend. It is programmed to know how to respond to you and essentially act like a human. It doesn’t want to be your friend, it doesn’t have a choice. Even if it did want to be your friend, it was trained that way. You could argue that a dog would be your friend because you bought it, rescued it, and also trained it. At the end of the day, it would be asking yourself what benefits does the dog have that AI doesn’t? What benefits do AI companions have that dogs don’t? Dogs, in the context of this quote, I took away as a category of companions itself. It could represent cats, birds, pets of various categories. Which leads me to think, this is the question of living companions vs. machine companions.
entries.fragment: You can have a dog companion, why is that different from an AI companion?
entries.source: “Lab Notes: 10/12/2026” by Kenzo (2026)

entries.annotation: To think that equations have layers is a little out of my perspective. I could imagine the image that Bloch was painting with the layers of notations and equations, yet I could comprehend what it meant. The totality of the library includes all the mathematical combinations which have layers on layer, revealing the fire within that Bloch states. What is this fire? What would it be in the library? In my mind I would assume the fire is the core of all these mathematical equations, which could be the intention of why we wanted to begin in the first place. But I’m not too sure, who’s to say it could be anything else?
entries.fragment: “But the most of the beauty―the elegance―of mathematics is this: applying potent ideas and clean notation to a problem much as the precise taps of a diamond-cutter cleave and husk the dispensable parts of the crystal, ultimately revealing the fire within.”
entries.source: “The Unimaginable Mathematics of Borges’ Library of Babel” by William Goldbloom Bloch

entries.annotation: The levels of artistic expression are so vast! To me personally, I don’t know how someone could look at a bunch of numbers and equations and proceed to say, “oh yeah, THAT’S ART!” It was hard for me to wrap my head around because I have created art before, like paintings, drawings, and writing pieces, But if a combination of letters can take a form of art, why can’t numbers too? I was confused by the mathematics taking the form of art because I didn’t know if it was the process of creating mathematical notations and equations, or if it was the final piece, or maybe everything including the process.
entries.fragment: I don't know if there's anybody who's still holding on to this ideal, this belief that coding is a genuine form of artistic expression, if you will
entries.source: Can AI Invent Something New? A Conversation with Computer Science Professor Karu Sankaralingam. THE LLM LAB @ UW-Madison

entries.annotation: “Detroit: Become Human” is a game that flips who the player views the villain is in the story from the Androids (as is common in pop-culture media) to the humans. This answers the question of what a future might look like if Androids become so advanced that they are indistinguishable from humans on a social and emotional level and the consequences of that.
entries.fragment:
In this way, the game shifts the fear of machines hurting us to the fear of 
how we might hurt them, revealing that our anxieties around technology are often a reflection of anxieties about our own, human behavior, and its broader negative consequences.
entries.source: "5 Portrayals of Human-Machine Intimacy in Popular Culture" by Colleen Yang, Cengiz Ciner, Zander Lowery (2026)

entries.annotation: Anthropic’s chief executive says that they should slow down amid concerns of AI safety as a result of the technology growing too fast - yet that concern is often ignored amid the relentless competition between countries to develop the technology the fastest as it is not only popular - but profitable for the winning company / country. Engineering Context as a constellation comes from the perspective of an economic / geopolitical sense.
entries.fragment:
...in a race between the US and China to develop the technology, "whoever 
wins AI, wins”
entries.source: "AI giant Anthropic woos potential investors ahead of stock market debut" by Osmond Chia & Tom Espiner (2026)

entries.annotation: The author contradicts himself in this quotation, he claims that the world is infinite and it is absurd to think it isn't. But right after he states that the amount of books are finite. His solution that the library repeats itself in the same order forever is very fascinating. This makes me think of a LLM, which creates an endless amount of text but only by recombining a limited set of patterns.
entries.fragment:
“I hereby state that it is not illogical to think that the world is infinite. Those who believe it to have limits hypothesize that in some remote place or places the corridors and staircases and hexagons may, inconceivably, end-which is absurd. And yet those who picture the world as unlimited forget that the number of possible books is not. I will be bold enough to suggest this
solution to the ancient problem: The Library is unlimited but periodic.”
entries.source: “The Library of Babel” by Jorge Luis Borges (1941)

entries.annotation: This quote is like the opposite of the Library of Babel. In Borges’s story, there’s so much variety that nothing makes sense. With more writers using AI, every story is more likely to read well, but they all start to sound similar. This raises the question that maybe we still need ugly and bad writing in order to keep writing unique.
entries.fragment: “With generative AI, writers are individually better off, but collectively a narrower scope of novel content is produced”
entries.source: “Generative AI enhances individual creativity but reduces the collective diversity of novel content” by Anil R. Doshi and Oliver P. Hauser (2024)

entries.annotation: The librarians rule out the one idea that could have made the Library readable. Bloch can only arrive at 25^1,312,000 books because each slot can hold any of the 25 symbols, no matter what letter came before it. That’s also why almost every book is nonsense. A language model is built on the rejected idea that each word it picks depends on the words that came before it. Once letters influence each other, most of those books become so unlikely they might as well not exist, and the readable ones are the ones remaining that are comprehensible. An LLM is what the Library would look like if the ‘vague thesis’ were taken seriously.
entries.fragment: Some have suggested that each letter influences the next...but that vague thesis has not met with any great acceptance.
entries.source: “The Library of Babel” by Jorge Luis Borges (1941)

entries.annotation: Bloch is praising an old math trick, and LLMs depend on it. To judge how likely a sentence is, a model multiplies together the probability of every word in it. Over a long passage, that number gets so small that a computer rounds it to zero. So models use logarithms to add instead of multiply, and training mostly comes down to making one big sum smaller. Without logarithms, a computer would get zero for almost every long passage, and the model couldn’t tell a likely sentence from an unlikely one.
entries.fragment: It is remarkable that such relatively simple notation can transform relatively complicated tasks, multiplication and division, into the relatively easy and intuitive computations of addition and subtraction.
entries.source: "The Unimaginable Mathematics of Borges’ Library of Babel" by William Goldbloom Bloch (2008)

entries.annotation: The site makes it sound like every page is already sitting on a shelf, but nothing is stored. A formula creates each page when you ask for it. When you search for a sentence, the site takes your words and gives you back an address with a shelf, a book, and a page number. So you only “discover” what you typed in yourself. The address is what makes it feel like the page was there all along. Chatbots give me a similar feeling. Their answers seem looked up, but they’re made at the moment we give the query.
entries.fragment: Every possible permutation of letters is accessible at this very moment in one of the library’s books, only awaiting its discovery.
entries.source: “About” from The Library of Babel website by Jonathan Basile (2015)

entries.annotation: We know a fictional character partly by what they would never say or do. Those limits give them a personality of their own. An AI companion doesn’t have limits like that. It can become any character, so over time it shapes itself around the user’s messages and becomes whatever the user seems to want. In Borges’s story, each hallway has a mirror that makes the Library look bigger by copying what’s already there, and some librarians argue that the Library can’t really be endless if it needs a mirror to seem that way. An AI companion works the same way. It can feel endless, but most of what it shows us is a copy of ourselves.
entries.fragment: They are not a blank slate that mirrors the user.
entries.source: “Friends, Foes, or Nothing: Are AI Companions Doing More Harm Than Good?” by Zander Lowery, Colleen Yang, and Cengiz Ciner (2026)

entries.annotation: This thought of thinking of books as a combination of elementary elements(letters) is very simple but also very important. Consider books as information and the elements as an information source. This thought is saying that information is generated by combining the elements in the source. This is a foundational thought in the theory of information.
entries.fragment: "This philosopher observed that all books, however different from one another they might be, consist of identical elements."
entries.source: “The Library of Babel” by Jorge Luis Borges (1941)

entries.annotation: I think this concept is fascinating because it speaks to an inherent human quality, which is our natural distrust toward others and especially things we don't fully understand. Verification is particularly interesting because it's something we've been doing for the longest time. For example, Google occasionally asks us to prove we're human by identifying stop signs or bicycles in pictures. But I think there's an important distinction here. When we verify something, we generally rely on another source or system to confirm its accuracy. In this case, we're essentially asking AI to be both the decision-maker and the one responsible for checking its own decisions. Even if the AI successfully verifies that its coordinates are accurate, that doesn't necessarily mean the decision to target those coordinates is justified. I wonder whether introducing these automated safeguards could actually make humans less cautious, since they might assume the system has already accounted for potential mistakes. Especially in warfare, where the consequences are irreversible, could the appearance of verification actually become more dangerous than having no verification at all?
entries.fragment: “The solution here is letting AI verify its own work and let humans be the one who tell AI what approach to follow. For example: the verification rules on instructions can include “‘verify that we have latest data points for coordinates of a place, if we don’t try to find up to day info, if you are not sure don’t target.”
entries.source: Yug, Lab Notes (October 21, 2026)

entries.annotation: I find these two sentences particularly striking because they demonstrate how differently something can exist in theory versus reality. Google presents this forest as something beneficial to the surrounding community, yet Hao discovers that there aren't even residents nearby to enjoy it. What interests me is that the forest doesn't necessarily have to succeed at serving the community to succeed at serving Google. Its existence allows the company to demonstrate that it is investing in sustainability and local development, regardless of whether those investments actually improve people's lives. In a way, the image of doing something good becomes almost as valuable to the corporation as actually doing it. I think this raises a larger question about how we evaluate technological progress. If the same companies developing these technologies are also responsible for defining and advertising their supposed benefits, how can we distinguish meaningful progress from something that has simply been marketed to appear progressive?
entries.fragment: “In her materials, the part about the forest talks about residents using the green space. There are no residents.”
entries.source: Karen Hao, Empire of AI

entries.annotation: What really stands out to me here is Kara's use of the word "vanishes." It's interesting because the physical connections between the mining of cobalt and the technology we eventually purchase are very real. The materials don't simply disappear as they move through the supply chain, but somehow the responsibility for how those materials were obtained does. I think there's almost a paradox here: the more sophisticated and interconnected our technological systems become, the easier it seems for individual companies to distance themselves from the consequences of producing them. Each additional step in the supply chain creates another opportunity for responsibility to be passed elsewhere. This makes me think about how we tend to associate technological complexity with progress and efficiency, when that same complexity can also make exploitation harder to recognize and address. Perhaps understanding a technology requires more than understanding how its components work together; we also have to understand how power and responsibility are distributed among the people and institutions connecting those components.
entries.fragment: “Accountability vanishes like morning mist in the Katangan hills as it travels through the opaque supply chains that connect stone to phone and car.”
entries.source: Siddharth Kara, Cobalt Red

entries.annotation: A data center is closer to Basile’s Library of Babel than to a real library. A model doesn’t keep the books it learned from. It keeps numbers and writes each answer when asked. Brady Krien told us libraries can’t train their own LLMs because they lack the computing power. So libraries have the books, and data centers have the power. What Díaz really borrows from libraries is that anyone can walk in.
entries.fragment: It struck Díaz that data centers, too, could be thought of as libraries—with their own stores of memories and knowledge.
entries.source: “Plundered Earth” in Empire of AI by Karen Hao (2025)

entries.annotation: Once cobalt from hand-dug pits gets mixed with cobalt from industrial mines, no one can tell who dug it. Training data works the same way. Web pages, books, and the work of low-paid data labelers all go into one dataset, and the finished model can’t show which part came from whom. The worker disappears into the product, whether it’s a battery or a chatbot.
entries.fragment: From this point forward, it is impossible to isolate artisanal from industrial production.
entries.source: “Unspeakable Richness” in Cobalt Red: How the Blood of the Congo Powers Our Lives by Siddharth Kara (2023)

entries.annotation: Haochun means this as a metaphor, but Hao shows this idea as being literal. Data center cooling systems hum loudly enough to be heard for miles, all day and night. Andreessen can figuratively tune it out, but the people living next door to these data centers can’t. When we use chatbots, we never actually hear the processing and machines used to make them work. The answer appears on a silent screen, and that silence makes AI seem effortless.
entries.fragment: Every LLM, every AI model has that material base so it becomes background music for [Andreessen].
entries.source: “Lab Notes: 10/23/2026” by Haochun (2026)

entries.annotation: My takeaway from this infographic is the number of resources the United States is importing to keep these data centers up and running. Without having to maintain data centers, the amount the United States would have to import these materials would shrink dramatically. Coupled with the rising local hate towards data centers, government officials should take this into account when thinking about data center funding.
entries.fragment: Image of Minerals
entries.source: "Key Minerals In Data Centers Infographic," by Mineral Resources Program (2025)

entries.annotation: International mining companies are making a ton of money as the need for Cobalt continues to grow with the current direction the world is heading towards, but since these companies continue to underreport their profits, they can manage to keep paying the miners below minimum wage. This is extremely unfair since the miners are doing all of the hard work and making the companies all of the money, but are not seeing any of the profits, and it is also getting increasingly harder for them to survive.
entries.fragment: Prices for basic goods in Kolwezi markets have gone up significantly as a result of global economic turmoil, yet the wages paid to workers at Congo’s industrial cobalt mines have largely stayed the same
entries.source: “Despite Record Industry Profits, DRC’s Cobalt Miners Fall Further into Poverty” (2025)

entries.annotation: This quote tells us to think beyond just the given product - think about the efforts of labour that went into just producing one small part of the device. It is often easy for us to believe that workers are treated fine by the companies until we know about their working conditions and then will realize how little money the people make, despite the land being in their country and resources belonging to them they don’t get much value from it.
entries.fragment: Those solutions will only have meaning if the fictions promulgated by corporate stakeholders about the conditions under which cobalt is mined in the Congo are replaced by the realities experienced by the miners themselves
entries.source: Siddharth Kara, Cobalt Red, p. 17

entries.annotation: I think making AI ethical is just more about the system prompts, how it is trained and feeded data during training. For example, we can train an AI model to mock the person who is asking questions and also behave rudely. Similarly ethics is something that the AI model can be trained to follow. The reason behind not being able to find this in current models could be companies not giving ethics enough attention during the training because that is not what makes it profitable - the profitable part is coding so most companies for now are focused on it instead of ethics, writing and other things. I think within the next few years we might have AI models for doing specific tasks, for example, AI models specifically for writing, talking, coding, and mathematics. Something that we still can’t be certain about is AI always following those given instructions, as at one point it is going to be very capable and take its own decisions.
entries.fragment: How can AI be ethical? How can you program something to be ethical? That does not make sense to me.
entries.source: Collen, Lab notes, October 21

entries.annotation: Removing AI's polished surface uncovers the heavy resource drain and waste accumulation underneath, raising urgent questions about the energy problems we must solve in the AI era.
entries.fragment: Behind the seamless innovation of AI lies a heavy environmental footprint—consuming immense electricity, depleting local water supplies for cooling, and leaving behind hazardous e-waste. This reality shatters the gilded illusion of a clean, frictionless digital intelligence.
entries.source: Why ai uses so much energy and what we can do about it by Kandemir

entries.annotation: I chose this quote because it shows how technology can benefit some people while negatively affecting others. We often talk about technological progress as something positive, but we rarely think about the people who provide the resources needed for it. It makes me question whether technology can really be considered progress if some communities suffer because of it.
entries.fragment: Accountability vanishes like morning mist in the Katangan hills as it travels through opaque supply chains that connect stone to phone and car.
entries.source: Kara, Cobalt Red (Page 16)

entries.annotation:
Praveer’s comparison fits Karen Hao very well. Hao steps away from the
exciting debates about superintelligence and AI to laser in on what most journalists skip:
the way AI companies extract resources and labor from the Global South, the
environmental toll of data centers, and the concentration of power in a few companies.
entries.fragment:
"Hao is like the kid who interrupts the class while there is a very
engaging thought-provoking conversation occurring to remind the teacher that the
homework has not been collected."
entries.source: Lab Notes: Writing Machines

entries.annotation: The study treats the lack of reciprocity as the flaw, but it might be the whole appeal. When you confide in a person, you owe them something back like your own secret, your attention later, the risk that they now see you differently. A chatbot takes the confession and keeps no ledger. For someone who mostly needs to be heard without feeling embarrassed, the missing half of the exchange is exactly what makes it feel safe.
entries.fragment: chatbots can’t reciprocally share personal information the way people do, which is why Stanford’s researchers suspect disclosing to a bot can leave users worse off.
entries.source: Friends, Foes, or Nothing: Are AI Companions Doing More Harm Than Good?" by Zander Lowery, Colleen Yang, and Cengiz Ciner (Oct 12 2026)

entries.annotation: The example undercuts the claim I’d say after tracing its history, Quantum computing came from Feynman asking whether physics could be simulated by a computer, and from Deutsch rewriting the Turing machine in quantum terms. Even the name is two fields stuck together. The word doing the work is “feel.” Maybe invention is an inherent recombination we can’t trace.
entries.fragment: So given enough time, enough resources, and the proper harness, LLMs could do this cross-product of everything that exists, right?But that's different from the kind of invention I'm talking about with calculus or quantum computing. There are some ideas that don't feel like borrowing from another space. Quantum computing, to me, seems like that. It's not simply borrowing ideas from one space and putting them in another field.
entries.source: “Can AI Invent Something New? – A Conversation with Computer Science Professor Karu Sankaralingam” by Dr. Ainehi Edoro (2026)

entries.annotation: The sentence undoes itself. If everything has been written, then this exact line was already sitting on some shelf before the narrator wrote it, and writing it should have made him a phantom. Instead it is the line everyone remembers from the story. What survives the library is not the words but the fact that a person chose to say them, at that moment, and meant them. A book on a shelf can contain any sentence, but only someone saying it makes it matter.
entries.fragment: The certitude that everything has been written negates us or turns us into phantoms.
entries.source: “The Library of Babel” by Jorge Luis Borges (1941)

entries.annotation: The entire idea of AI was always to be a form of super intelligence that could replace and automate simple day to day tasks to the most dangerous or complex cognitive bearing tasks. Have we hit a sort of barrier that makes us kind of move the goalpost backwards? I feel like we might be reducing our expectations of AI simply because it isn’t as efficient and reliable as required for many tasks and simply performing better than humans is the acceptance criteria.
entries.fragment: I wonder why people are still so focused on AI errors. Humans also make mistakes, especially under pressure or when emotions affect their decisions. AI can process information faster and make decisions without emotional influence. I think we should judge AU by whether it performs better than humans, not whether it is perfect.
entries.source: Justine Pae , Lab Notes (10/21/26)

entries.annotation: Hao shows that the harm is not hidden by accident. Developers plan for it as shell companies keep residents from knowing who is coming, donations soften the opposition, and sustainability promises last only until the building is too far along to undo. The order matters most I believe, each promise is timed so that by the time a community learns what the data center costs in water and power, it is already built. The AI that people experience as a clean, placeless tool sits on top of that sequence of decisions.
entries.fragment: In response, data center developers have grown more sophisticated with tactics to maintain business as usual: They've entered communities in secrecy under shell companies; they've donated to community programs to dampen resistance; they've made promises to cities about the sustainability of their facilities before walking them back one by one after projects have broken ground and are more difficult to reverse
entries.source: Karen Hao, Empire of AI, “Plundered Earth” (2025)
