entries.annotation: What stands out is that Kara treats accountability as something that disappears with distance. Each step from the pit in Kolwezi to the depot, the refiner, the battery maker, and the phone company adds another party who can say the problem happened somewhere else. “Stone to phone and car” compresses that whole journey into a few words, and it makes a phone feel less like a finished object and more like the last stop on a very long route. The same is true of anything that runs on these batteries and the data centers behind them.
entries.fragment: Accountability vanishes like morning mist in the Katangan hills as it travels through the opaque supply chains that connect stone to phone and car.
entries.source: Siddharth Kara, Cobalt Red, “Unspeakable Richness,” p. 16

entries.annotation: Professor Edoro describes Ifá in the same spatial vocabulary we used for embeddings: address, coordinate, memory space. The difference is how each system lands on a point. Instagram’s user model computes your coordinate from thousands of  past interactions, so your location is a summary of where you have already been. The Odu is cast with palm nuts and nobody controls the outcome. Both are geometries of stored knowledge, but only one lets chance choose the location, and that randomness is what keeps the whole archive in circulation instead of collapsing onto the verses the babalawo already knows best.
entries.fragment: In computer science terms, an Odu functions as an address: a fixed coordinate within a memory space pointing to a specific location where content is stored and retrieved.
entries.source: African Literary Studies in the Forest of the Digital” by Ainehi Edoro (2026)

entries.annotation: European geomancers inherited a rule-based system and could not accept that fixed rules might produce surprise, so they bolted on a spinning wheel. LLMs essentially make the same move where the model computes the same probability distribution every time, and a sampler adds randomness afterward so the output does not loop. The Bamana diviners got their variety from the rules themselves, since a simple odd or even rule, repeated over and over on just four random drawings, produces all the other symbols. Temperature might be our version of the wheel, a sign that we still treat determinism and unpredictability as opposites.
entries.fragment: By mounting the 16 figures on a wheel and spinning it, they maintained their society’s exclusion of any connections between determinism and unpredictability.
entries.source: “African Fractals: Modern Computing and Indigenous Design” by Ron Eglash (1999)

entries.annotation: The word that stands out is “guardianship.” A chatbot is also a single gateway to a huge corpus, and the company that runs it decides what comes through by setting the training data, the filters and the system prompt. Ifá splits these roles by making chance to pick the address, the babalawo recites the verses, and the client decides which one applies to her life. No one person guards the whole gate, and Soyinka suggests that anyone who claims to is a fool.
entries.fragment: Go to the orisa. None but fools / Claim guardianship of the final gateway
entries.source: “Samarkand and Other Markets I Have Known” by Wole Soyinka (2002)

entries.annotation: This quote is fascinating because it makes me question if we can measure everything in numbers including what someone hates, likes and other general things. It is possible to count a few things like how many movies has someone watched but something that I have never understood is how feeling is related to a number, for example, when someone asks you how happy are you from scale of 1 to 10 - i don’t know how to answer this because what does 5 mean here? that I’m half happy, but there is no such thing as being half happy. Similarly, AI is thought of as something that understands a lot of patterns but I do think what kind of data has been trained on and how confidently we can say it understands those patterns, for example understanding how happy a person is from their facial expressions by AI. LLMs will just do some mathematical calculations and then try to find the probability of how happy the person is. So, I believe that we can use numbers to just get an estimate and not exact patterns and understanding of feelings.
entries.fragment: Let who can, count the motes in a sunbeam / Or weigh the span of grief from voice to voice
entries.source: Samarkand and Other Markets I Have Known, Wole Soyinka (2002)

entries.annotation: This quote has a very deep meaning. We need to think about this because I see engineers in AI companies are spending a lot of money on tokens. Using AI to create prototypes, features and bug fixes. These tokens are really expensive and companies have to spend millions of dollars on them, but the question is whether all of this is worth spending because at the end of the day if a company is spending 200 million dollars on AI then they at least expect 250 million dollars more in return. One of the other concerns regarding this is the loss of creativity for example, earlier when I had to create an image I would spend time thinking about the image and then draw a rough sketch on the page, ask other about ideas and keep on iterating over it, but now all i have to do is write a prompt and ai creates an image. This is where the creativity is lost - no matter how descriptive the prompt is - LLMs will generate a particular kind of design which then stays in the user mind and they try to iterate around those ideas which then results in loss of creativity. This makes me question what is counted as the benefit of using AI - is it that the engineers were able to come up with the prototype quickly. But this resulted in narrowing down the ideas they could explore without using LLMs. I believe that instead of using AI to do the work fast we should rather focus on doing it even more slowly or at least take the same amount of time it would take the task to complete without AI, but with the highest quality possible as we now have someone who can give us feedback constantly without getting tired.
entries.fragment: This pushes us to scale models cautiously with ROI (return on investment) in mind.
entries.source: Lyu et al, Extremely Long User History Modeling at Instagram, p. 1

entries.annotation:
The discussion we had about LLMs connecting words in space and then the library of Babel and the books being nonsensical all look like this figure right here to me. Like all the 2D words and texts we created with our human brains are just diffraction patterns to AI and it makes an Ewald sphere out of them to make a possible 3D map of a sentence which might be wrong and only logical but it is all the AI can do, and we just try to fit our
thoughts and opinions into it, because we want to believe it did it right.
entries.fragment: The Ewald Sphere: According to Wikipedia, “The Ewald sphere is a geometric construction used in electron, neutron, and x-ray diffraction which shows the relationship between: the wavevector of the incident and diffracted beams, the diffraction angle for a given reflection, the reciprocal lattice of the crystal.”

entries.annotation:
YES. Use AI, talk to it, vent to it. Listen to it maybe when it calms you down so you can go talk to your human companions about your issues calmly. But talking to a machine about your problems and listening to its advice and not putting your brain into it is just stupid. How could you take emotional and social advice from a machine that has never interacted in an
emotional/social environment? The problem is not the chatbots talking about your feelings or trying to be your friends, the problem is us humans depending on them and closing up in our shell and getting lazy to get out of our rooms and say hi to people around us.
entries.fragment: The bots [AI companions] only become an issue when someone solely starts depending on them for companionship
entries.source: Friends, Foes, or Nothing: Are AI Companions Doing More Harm Than Good?

entries.annotation: Is that all that God is supposed to be? An all knowing person? Someone who knows everything about the universe? The word for that is omniscient, also used as one of the qualities of God, along with omnipotent, omnipresent and omnibenevolent. Maybe don't reduce God to just one of His supposed qualities. Or don't use words like “analogous to a God”. I don't question the idea of the Book-Man, I question his ability to be analogous to God.
entries.fragment: the Book-Man...this librarian is analogous to a god.
entries.source: Borges, “The Library of Babel”

entries.annotation:
This is what comes to my mind when I read about AI being used in warfare and to increase the speed and efficiency of target detection. AI is not accurate enough to know who is a civilian and who is a target. Yet. Maybe when we reach a point in time where AI can do this process with 100% accuracy, we can come back to this discussion again; because even one
innocent civilian life counts.
entries.fragment: The Blackstone's formulation, stated by the English jurist William Blackstone in his seminal work Commentaries on the Laws of England in the 1760s, is: “It is better that ten guilty persons escape than that one innocent suffer.”
entries.source: Blackstone's ratio

entries.annotation: Acknowledgement. That’s what the families and loved ones get. For losing their children, parents and friends.
entries.fragment: In that [2021 Kabul drone strike disaster] incident, a U.S. drone strike killed ten civilians, and the Department of Defense later acknowledged that it was a tragic mistake.
entries.source: The Pursuit of Speed in AI Warfare

entries.annotation: Is nobody pausing to wonder how much that energy and electricity means to people who don't have access to electricity? This could be used to light up homes in villages, classes in school, make electricity cheaper for countries and places that don't have the money to pay for electricity. A country’s worth of electricity for creating something that’s supposed to help humans and make human life easier is insanity.
entries.fragment: By 2030, at the current pace of growth, data centres are projected to use 8% of the country’s power …. AI computing globally could use more energy than all of India, the world’s third-largest electricity consumer.
entries.source: Karen Hao’s Empire of AI, Plundered Earth

entries.annotation:
Man always wants more. Man has built this life all by asking for more. This
seeking has led to AI and will lead to the world of technoutopia or technodestruction. We’ll find out soon and man won’t stop seeking no matter the outcome.
entries.fragment: Man is restless seeker
entries.source: Wole Soyinka, "Samarkand and Other Markets I Have Known”

entries.annotation:
I liked how they were willing to hold on to the secrets of the trade, not for
money. Only when they understood the significance of cross-cultural math and specifically saw the recursive construction of the Cantor set were they willing to explain their tricks. You could tell how much they love and respect their divination system.
entries.fragment:
But when I finally asked how he derived the symbols …. My offers of
increasingly high payments were met with disinterest
entries.source: Eglash - African Fractals

entries.annotation:
This made me think about whether AI can actually come up with something
completely new or if it's just combining ideas that already exist. I think there's still a difference between AI and human creativity.
entries.fragment: There are some ideas that don’t feel like borrowing from another space.
entries.source: Professor Karu Sankaralingam, Interview

entries.annotation:
I like the growth and adaptation that has been reflected in this system. The
world is split in two - anti-AI and pro-AI. But its the people who have looked into AI with open minds and taken cautious steps are the ones who’re getting the best of both worlds. These people will use AI and learn to make their life and work easier but also know moderation.
entries.fragment: I think the entire computer programming community went through all our stages of grief, and we’ve accepted it.
entries.source: Can AI Invent Something New? – A Conversation with Computer Science Professor Karu Sankaralingam

entries.annotation:
I found it interesting how African knowledge can be left out of the history of
technology without anyone directly saying it doesn't matter. It made me question how much of AI's history we're actually learning.
entries.fragment: This is a colonial structure that operates through non-recognition rather than misrecognition.
entries.source: Ainehi Edoro, In the Forest of the Digital (Page 2)

entries.annotation: This made me wonder how AI can understand emotions when they can't really be measured. Maybe there are parts of being human that numbers and algorithms will never fully capture.
entries.fragment: It’s impossible to make a scale of human emotion.
entries.source: Kenzo, Lab Notes: October 28

entries.annotation:
How do we know it's a stable navigation? What is the measure? Isn't there
a high possibility that the verses for each Odu are much more different now than what they’re meant to be. I appreciate the beauty of the system, it evolves and grows with time. But what about authenticity? How do we check for that?
entries.fragment: The durability of the archive therefore resides less in identical content than in a stable navigational structure that keeps the system traversable across generations.
entries.source: Ainehi Edoro - In the Forest of the Digital, Act II

entries.annotation:
The current situation in the world regarding AI has all the hallmarks of the
definition of moral panics. Exaggeration. Policy Making. Political Involvement. Media Hype. Deviant socio-cultural behavior. The only thing new is that we’re not scared of a “special” group of people, but of something a different “special” group of people built.
entries.fragment:
Moral Panic - A mass movement based on the exaggerated perception that
some cultural behaviour or group of people is dangerously deviant and poses a threat to society's values and interests.
entries.source: Oxford Reference, Moral Panic

entries.annotation: I mean seeing a robot dance has its fascinating aspects, but I think a big part is understanding that the dance moves were programmed by people who researched dance or knew how to dance. I saw this youtube short a bit ago and thought to myself, “I wonder why are people so impressed?” The technology behind the programming and coding is very fascinating, but if a robot does something a human can, why is it all of a sudden amazing and even better?
entries.fragment: A YouTube short video of a robot dancing at the AI world conference.
entries.source: Robot Dancing at AI world conference (2026) YouTube short video

entries.annotation: Here we need to stop about technology and the purposes we have in the first place. Soyinka was essentially telling us to think about what technology cannot do, and that made me sit for a while. What can’t technology do? Society always praises technology in a way where it will be our savior and something that will save the world from all the problems humans have created. But why? Why do we put so much faith into something digital? And why can’t we also see the importance of what it can’t measure. In my opinion, I see that technology cannot measure love, gratitude, and feelings. Those are on a scale even humans and beings sometimes cannot fathom in light of determining how vast emotions are. What is left that AI can’t do that we may still need to keep a close eye on?
entries.fragment: [Soyinka’s] phrase about the sunbeam and motes made me think more about the limitations of technology. Does technology measure emotions? How do LLMs think of humans? Does it think that we are emotional? Can technology account for the quiet individual here?
entries.source: “Lab Notes: 10/28/2026” by Colleen (2026)

entries.annotation: I will say before I read this article, I already had my biases about LLMs and the coding aspect of GPT2. The idea that this perfect encoder/decoder world could add context to any word based on the words added after it I found a little skeptical. It still can’t understand the sentence just by definition? I think that’s something people also miss at first as well. We have LLMs and so much coding and effort is put in to help with advancements, but it can still not determine the meaning of one word by definition and is solely trying to use context. I find that confusing.
entries.fragment: The GPT2, and some later models like TransformerXL and XLNet are auto-regressive in nature. BERT is not. That is a trade off. In losing auto-regression, BERT gained the ability to incorporate the context on both sides of a word to gain better results. XLNet brings back autoregression while finding an alternative way to incorporate the context on both sides.
entries.source: The Illustrated GPT-2 (Visualizing Transformer Language Models) by Jay Alammar (August 20, 2019)

entries.annotation: What is the final gateway? Is it an end goal that isn’t supposed to be guarded by individuals who also want to reach the end, I suppose, too? We have these companies who put a lot of money into digital advancement and the AI race within the world. We see millionaires and billionaires get so much money, but these companies charge people like 80 dollars to have a subscription on Claude or ChatGPT. Not to say all millionaires and billionaires are fools for blocking the “final gateway.” or the path where humans can advance these digital works without the limitations of other factors, but take that as you will. Companies, states, countries, and others claim AI. But who owns it? Will it be owned by the companies whose workers add to the advancements, or the billionaire who’s invested the most, or the hard working miners looking for parts in Africa, or the government trying to identify individuals on the streets with Flock camera, or will it be for the community and the people.
entries.fragment: None but fools/Claim guardianship of the final gateway
entries.source: Samarkand and Other Markets I Have Known, Wole Soyinka (2002)

entries.annotation: Recent advances in AI's cybersecurity capabilities are changing cybersecurity. In the past, the ability to identify vulnerabilities and develop exploits was considered one of the most important skills for security experts. However, as AI becomes increasingly capable of performing these tasks. So now what is the core capability of security experts.
entries.fragment: Anthropic described the Linux exploit in an October 27 post about flaws that its AI model, Claude, found and exploited. The Hacker News covered the post on October 28. Claude wrote the exploit after "initial prompting," Anthropic said.

entries.annotation:
GPT-2 is trained to simply predict the next token, yet it can
produce surprisingly complex and coherent text. I find the gap between such
a simple objective and its sophisticated behavior fascinating. It makes me
wonder how much intelligence can emerge from optimizing simple rules at a
large scale.
entries.fragment:
The way these models actually work is that after each token is
produced, that token is added to the sequence of inputs.”
entries.source: Jay Alammar, The Illustrated GPT-2

entries.annotation:
Geometry here is more than shapes; it offers a way to understand
growth and self-organization. It makes me wonder what other mathematical
insights might be hidden in cultural practices.
entries.fragment:
Since cellular automata model the emergence of such patterns in
complex scientific studies of living systems, and certain Ghanaian log spirals
have long been regarded as generalized models for organic growth, it is not
unreasonable to consider the possibility that the self-organizing dynamics
observable in oware are also linked to concepts of biological morphogenesis
in traditional Ghanaian knowledge systems.
entries.source: Eglash, African Fractals

entries.annotation:
The same material can mean innovation and profit for some, but
exploitation for others. Technological progress doesn’t always create new
value for everyone, sometimes it just shifts the costs to those with the least
power.
entries.fragment:
The global cobalt supply chain is the mechanism that transforms the
dollar-a-day wages of the Congo’s artisanal miners into multibillion-dollar
quarterly profits at the top of the chain.
entries.source: Siddharth Kara, Cobalt Red

entries.annotation:
An algorithm can perfectly optimize its objective while producing
terrible outcomes. The real question is not just how efficiently AI makes
decisions, but who defines the objective and decides which trade-offs are
acceptable. Who should be responsible for the decisions?
entries.fragment:
When a system is optimized using ‘decision-making speed’ as its sole
objective function, existing multi-layered human verification procedures
(Human-in-the-Loop) are treated as the factor that is causing the risk of delay
by hindering speed.
entries.source: Roh, Jin, and Tiwari, The Pursuit of Speed in AI Warfare a.

entries.annotation: The significance of an individual element is not fixed but emerges from its relationships with other elements. When we extract something from its original context and place it somewhere else, are we simply revealing a meaning that was already there, or are we actively creating a new one? This problem is also closely related to rights of content creators.
entries.fragment:
The elements are dynamically interdependent within an operating
system.
entries.source: Augmenting Human Intellect: A Conceptual Framework by Douglas C. Engelbart (1962)

entries.annotation:
The number of books and possible combinations of the
knowledge is enormous for human-being. They’re not something that
could be processed in human life time span. However, with the help of
LLM, this might be different.
entries.fragment:
The number of books in the Library, although easily notated, is
unimaginable.
entries.source: Bloch, The Unimaginable Mathematics of Borges' Library of Babel

entries.annotation: Sankaralingam says a chip designed by AI would go unbuilt, even if it beat human designs on every measure. The surprise is that the discomfort would persist even if you fully understood the design. Thus, he is saying that authorship is more important than understanding when it comes to the adaptation of a technology. Compare this to Lyu’s paper where he suggests ROI (Return on investment) is the only judge. Or the fact that the more advanced LLMs become, the less we know what is going on in the “black box.” There seems to be a contradiction here
entries.fragment: If a Gen AI system came up with the design of a chip… very few companies would go build that…. My theory is that even if you came up with that full understanding, you would still have a weird sense of discomfort because you didn’t come up with it.
entries.source: Can AI Invent Something New? - A Conversation with Computer Science Professor Karu Sankaralingam” by Ainehi Edoro and students in English 178 (2026)

entries.annotation: The way the world is going, humans have less and less of a role compared to computers. The Ifa way of thinking would completely disagree with this, it sees AI as important only as assistance to humans, and it shouldn’t be replacing anything. The Ifa way of thinking argues that LLMs standing alone, would be useless which is where we are almost at as a society.
entries.fragment: Ifá insists on social interpretation, embedding consultation and dialogue, not replacing it. Ifá demonstrates that an algorithm can never stand alone . The Ifá algorithm is incomplete without interpretation, dialogue, and moral responsibility
entries.source: "What Ifá, an Indigenous binary knowledge system can teach us about AI” by Uyiosa Omoregie (2025)

entries.annotation:
The author compares AI to your basic keyboard autocomplete. Comparing
AI and this very familiar technology to everyone allows LLms to feel more familiar to
most people. But it brings up an interesting point. If autocomplete and ChatGPT run on
the same basic idea, then large language models are just really very powerful
autocomplete. Does this make predicting the next word the same thing as auto
complete?
entries.fragment:
“The most famous language models are smartphone keyboards that suggest the
next word based on what you’ve currently typed.”
entries.source: “The Illustrated GPT-2 (Visualizing Transformer Language Models)” by Jay Alammar (2019)

entries.annotation: This is how the report suggests what Meta's view of its new “Your Algorithm” dashboard is, which shows you your interests and lets you nudge them in different directions. It tells us that the feature is meant to reassure (“peace of mind”) more than to actually steer. Compare this to Ifá, where the client has the power to interrupt the babalawo and decide whether a verse fits their life. The feature lets you see more or less of a topic, but not that “the verse is not me."
entries.fragment:
Meta sees the feature primarily as a reassurance mechanism— an option
people want for peace of mind, even if they seldom use it
entries.source: “Instagram Rolls Out New ‘Your Algorithm’ Controls For U.S. Reels Users” by RTTNews (2025)

entries.annotation:
This quote describes something I see on my own phone all the time. If I
watch a few food videos, Instagram shows me more food videos, and the more I watch
them, the more it wants me to watch food videos. The author calls this a loop because
the app looks at what I already like and just gives me more of it, so it never really lets
me explore new things and become a different person. This contrasts with Ifá, because
it’s supposed to show you something new instead of just repeating things you already
know.
entries.fragment:
“Prediction closes the loop by feeding the user back into increasingly refined
versions of themselves.”
entries.source: “In the Forest of the Digital” by Ainehi Edoro (2026)

entries.annotation: I like how Turing makes this comparison because it shows that we, humans, are different from machines. We don’t need to compare all aspects between a computer and a human but we do need to ask the questions on what differentiates humans from machines.
entries.fragment: We do not wish to penalize the machine for its inability to shine in beauty competitions, nor to penalize a man for losing in a race against an aeroplane.
entries.source: "Computing Machinery and Intelligence” by Alan Turing (1950)

entries.annotation: The question of whether technology can measure emotions stuck out to me here. It is clear that, as mentioned in the DV365 paper, certain technologies can measure a “quiet individual” using other methods. In the case of Instagram, someone who only scrolls still produces data through how fast that person scrolls and how long they stay. Whether or not they interact with the content is irrelevant - they are still producing data. Outside of Instagram, I wonder what other methods could be used to turn the everyday actions of another into data.
entries.fragment: [Soyinka’s] phrase about the sunbeam and motes made me think more about the limitations of technology. Does technology measure emotions? How do LLMs think of humans? Does it think that we are emotional? Can technology account for the quiet individual here?
entries.source: Lab Notes (10/28) By Colleen

entries.annotation:
This quote is a great representation of AI. AI is great at making something
that already exists better, just like a candle that burns longer and costs less, but it can't
come up with a totally new idea like the lightbulb. We still need humans for that kind of
game-changing, next level idea.
entries.fragment:
Imagine you have a candle. If you tell AI to improve it, you’ll get a candle that
shines brighter and longer, costs less, and probably has the best design,” Gerlich said. “But AI will not make the leap from candle to light bulb. That is out-of-the-box thinking—a type of creative thinking that AI, which is based on pattern recognition, cannot do.
entries.source: “How AI Is Reshaping Human Skills and Thinking” by Zara Abrams (2026)

entries.annotation: Drawing the connection between how we learn and connecting it to how a computer works shows the beauty of computers. Where a machine learning model does millions of simulations to figure out the most ideal way to go about a problem, us humans go through these simulations of trial and error until we learn the rules set for us. The way humans and artificial intelligence learn might be more similar than we think.
entries.fragment: I wonder if young children also learn this specific way. Children have to look at letters and memorize the letters, children follow rules and know numbers have value in place.
entries.source: Colleen

entries.annotation: This quote makes me think about the relationship between AI and human responsibility. AI can follow instructions and make decisions much faster than humans, but that does not mean humans should give up responsibility for the results. I chose Following Rules because it raises questions about what happens when machines follow rules that humans create.
entries.fragment: Delegating a task does not necessarily mean delegating responsibility.
entries.source: The LLM Lab @ UW-Madison

entries.annotation: I love this quote because it explains how something easily created can be beautiful but doesn’t necessarily make it beautiful. My first thought was how everyone can pick up a paintbrush and draw on a page. Everyone can draw a line multiple times until their piece is complete. But, this doesn’t make every piece a stroke of genius. The tool doesn’t make you a genius, it’s how you use the tool that will make you a genius.
entries.fragment: A technology can make production ubiquitous without making artistic achievement ubiquitous.
entries.source: Seeing Beeple’s Diffuse Control in Madison, WI

entries.annotation: This quote reminds me that technology can be understood through different cultural perspectives. I found it interesting that traditional African knowledge systems can offer new ways of thinking about modern AI. I chose Country of Geniuses because it encourages us to imagine a future where AI is shaped by diverse ideas and ways of understanding the world.
entries.fragment: We are here to ask why it appears given that everything digital, from a genealogical perspective, is western. Can we speak of an African digital gnosis?
entries.source: Edoro

entries.annotation: This quote makes me think about how technology is changing the way we process information. Social media algorithms are becoming better at predicting what keeps us engaged, but that does not necessarily mean they help us learn. I chose The Moving Goalpost because it makes us question whether technological intelligence should be measured by its ability to predict our behavior or help us understand the world.
entries.fragment: Social media as a whole does have the tendency to push users into a wormhole of feeling emotions rather than processing new information.
entries.source: Writing Machines Lab Notes (Nikhil, 10/28)

entries.annotation: If someone was to mention a pope and AI model in the same sentence, I would think that they were trying to set up a joke. Sadly this is not the case; Anthropic has a department that is researching putting empathy and morality inside their AI models. This poses the question, is this a necessary procession we need to take when continuing our development of AI or is it a sign that we need to turn around and stop creating thinking machines.
entries.fragment: Anthropic, one of the fastest-growing technology companies in the world, had turned to one of humanity’s most ancient sources of wisdom to help determine how to train its A.I. models to behave virtuously
entries.source: The New York Times

entries.annotation: I can’t believe that AI, right now, has this capability to break into a server without the helping hand of a human. If there are actions that AI are taking that we can’t explain, we need to take a step back. Overall we need to be holding the company accountable for the AI they are creating
entries.fragment: The issue erupted in July when OpenAI revealed that a swarm of its AI agents escaped from a testing ground and used stolen credentials to break into the servers of Hugging Face, an AI development hub and marketplace, to obtain information needed for a task

entries.annotation:
Where we talk and communicate with words, LLMs talk and communicate with numbers and signals. Since we don’t have strict rules for what thinking is, are LLMs even thinking or just processing information. Are human rules and standards translatable to computers and other
animals?
entries.fragment: LLMs think but not in a human way. They think but not as humans

entries.annotation: Alammar explains GPT-2 through something most of us have done. We keep tapping the middle suggestion on our phone keyboard until the sentence starts going in circles. The way out is to pick a word the machine didn’t rank first. GPT-2 does this with a setting called top-k, which lets it choose from its top 40 words instead of always taking number one. Dr. Edoro mentioned how the random cast in Ifá does a similar job, so the babalawo doesn’t keep returning to the verses he knows best. I wonder what a top-k setting would look like on my Reels feed.
entries.fragment: it sometimes can stuck in repetitive loops where the only way out is if you click the second or third suggested word.
entries.source: “The Illustrated GPT-2 (Visualizing Transformer Language Models)” by Jay Alammar (2019)

entries.annotation: In Bamana sand divination, only the first four marks are random, and a fixed rule builds the rest of the reading. When European geomancers borrowed the same 16 figures, they put them on a spinning wheel and turned the whole reading into luck. The figures stayed the same, but moving them into a new setup changed what they meant, which is a lot like what we do when we move quotes into constellations.
entries.fragment: By mounting the 16 figures on a wheel and spinning it, they maintained their society’s exclusion of any connections between determinism and unpredictability.
entries.source: “Numeric Systems” in African Fractals: Modern Computing and Indigenous Design by Ron Eglash (1999)

entries.annotation: Instagram opens by telling users that their interests change. Six months earlier, Instagram’s engineers published the DV365 paper, which assumes the opposite. Their “Stable Interest Hypothesis” says the most useful part of a user’s history is the part that stays the same, and they found that the numbers representing a user were still over 90% similar after a week. The new panel lets us edit a short list of topics, but the announcement never says whether those edits reach the history underneath. The feature sounds like control, but I’m not sure how much it actually changes our algorithm.
entries.fragment: Your interests change – and now using AI, your algorithm can change with you.
entries.source: “Introducing a new way to see and control your algorithm” by Instagram (2025)

entries.annotation: Turing’s human computer had no authority to deviate from its rules. Sankaralingam says a modern chip deviates all the time. It runs instructions out of order and guesses which way the program will go, then throws the work away if the guess was wrong. We never notice because the final answer comes out the same as if it had followed our order. I find it interesting that even the hardware under an LLM is making predictions based on what happened before, the same way Instagram predicts what we’ll watch next.
entries.fragment: A modern computer doesn’t actually run it in the order in which you told it to.
entries.source: “Can AI Invent Something New? – A Conversation with Computer Science Professor Karu Sankaralingam” by Ainehi Edoro and English 178 students (2026)

entries.annotation: Kenzo says it’s impossible, but Instagram’s engineers built a scale from watch time in their DV365 paper. In the paper’s examples, watching a video for under 3 seconds counts as negative engagement and over 15 seconds counts as positive. The engineers even adjust for video length, since people stay longer on longer videos. Boredom, grief, and fascination could all keep me on a video for 16 seconds, and the paper would count them the same way. Soyinka warns against anyone who tries to weigh the span of grief, and this is the best example of emotions being used to manipulate engagement.
entries.fragment: It’s impossible to make a scale of human emotion.
entries.source: “Lab Notes: 10/28/2026” by Kenzo (2026)

entries.annotation:
Mist belongs to the same category as Hao’s “cloud” such that both are
vapor-like words for systems that are hidden. They have no creator, no author, and nobody can decide for it to go away.
entries.fragment: Accountability vanishes like morning mist in the Katangan hills
entries.source: “Unspeakable Richness” (Chapter 1, Cobalt Red) by Siddharth Kara (2023)

entries.annotation:
Background music is something that exists, but is drowned out in favor of
other sounds. Andreessen’s picture of AI looks perfect partly because the material base has been turned into something you "drown out." Datacenters let out a constant hum that people can hear for miles, around the clock. That same infrastructure comes off as "background music" for one person, yet relentless noise for others, and how loud it sounds depends on where you live and, in a way, position in life / wealth.
entries.fragment: It is not that Andreessen does not realize or care about the material base of AI, but instead, every LLM, every AI model has that material base so it becomes background music for him.
entries.source: Haochun - 10/23 Lab Notes
